config.title: Berlin Hiking Trails - FAQ
config.subtitle: What the twenty green routes are, where the trains meet them, and what changes once the clocks go back.

items.q: Are there real hiking trails in Berlin?
items.a: Yes, twenty of them, and they are official. The Senate has been plotting and waymarking the Grüne Hauptwege since 2004, and the marked network now covers about 575 km. Each route has a number from 1 to 20 and a name taken from the landscape it crosses, from the 7 km Bullengrabenweg in Spandau to the 63 km Spreeweg that runs from the Staaken border out to Erkner. Eighteen cross the city from edge to edge. Two are rings, the Innerer Parkring at 52 km and the Tiergartenring at 23 km. The waymark is a small white hiking bear on a green square.

items.q: Can you reach the Berlin green routes without a car?
items.a: Almost everywhere, and that is the useful part. Counting a station as on a route when it sits within 1 km of the line, 282 station points touch the twenty routes, across 195 different S-Bahn, U-Bahn and regional stations. Every pair of stations on the same route is a possible walk, which comes to 3,684 of them, and about 1,883 land between 2 and 12 km. That is why nobody needs to walk a whole route: you walk one station-to-station stage and take the train home from the other end.

items.q: Which Grüne Hauptweg should I walk first?
items.a: The Tiergartenring, Weg 19. It has 28 stations on 23 km and the widest gap between two of them is 2.5 km, so you can stop whenever you have had enough. A good first bite is S Tiergarten round to U Eberswalder Straße, about 10 km through the Hansaviertel, the Spreebogen, the Bernauer Straße end of Mauerpark and Prenzlauer Berg. If you want it to feel less like the city, Weg 14 from U Kaulsdorf-Nord to S Wuhlheide is roughly 7 km down a stream valley with Highland cattle in it.

items.q: Which routes are hard to reach by train?
items.a: Three stand out. The Spandauer Weg, Weg 2, has exactly two stations near its 33 km and the first 16.7 km has none, so it starts at a ferry landing and ends at a bus stop. The Barnimer Dörferweg, Weg 13, has five stations on 34 km with 16.7 km between S Karow and S Waidmannslust. The Dahmeweg, Weg 9, has three on 21 km and nothing at all for the last 11.9 km after S Grünau. Only eight of the twenty routes have a rail station at both official ends.

items.q: Are the Grüne Hauptwege signposted well enough to follow without a map?
items.a: Nearly, but the Senate itself advises carrying a map. Each route gets fixed signposts with full direction arms plus stickers between them, and the last six routes, numbers 1, 5, 7, 15, 16 and 17, were scheduled for their signs between March and summer 2026. Vandalism and building sites take individual markers out. All twenty routes are published as GPX, KML and printable PDF on the Senate's download page, so put the file on your phone before you leave.

items.q: What changes on these paths in autumn and winter?
items.a: Light, gates and ground. Sunset in Berlin is 19:28 on 13 September, 17:54 on 24 October, and 16:52 on 25 October once the clocks go back, then 16:15 by mid-November. The Senate describes the lighting on these routes as poor or missing, so plan to finish early. Several routes cross fenced ground that locks up in the evening: Tempelhofer Feld, which starts and ends the Innerer Parkring, closes at 21:30 through September and at 19:00 from 1 October. And the maintenance tracks along the Wuhle, the Panke and the canals turn heavy after a wet week.

items.q: Are the green routes suitable for a buggy or a wheelchair?
items.a: The official answer is no. The Senate states plainly that the Grüne Hauptwege are not barrier free. They are hiking routes, and especially in the outer districts they can include steps, high kerbs, soft or unsurfaced ground on waterway maintenance tracks, and poor or missing lighting, with no claim to extra traffic safety. Individual inner-city sections are smooth pavement or asphalt, the Teltowkanalweg being the most consistently firm, but the network as a whole is not designed for wheels.
